# Shrinkage Trades Variance for Bias

Ordinary least squares can be unstable when predictors are numerous or strongly
correlated. A small change in the outcomes may then produce a large change in
individual coefficients even when fitted values barely move. Ridge regression
stabilizes the fit by preferring coefficient vectors with small squared norm.

This preference deliberately introduces bias. The gain is often lower sampling
variance and better prediction for new experimental units. Ridge regression does
not make a confounded effect identifiable, prove causality, or reveal a unique
biological mechanism among correlated features. Its target is a regularized
prediction rule under an explicitly chosen loss and penalty.

# Data-generating Model and Prediction Target

For independent units $i=1,\ldots,n$, consider

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\mathbf x_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
E(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf x_i)=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf x_i)=\sigma^2.
$$

The rows of the $n\times p$ matrix $\mathbf X$ contain predictors. The
conditional mean is $\beta_0+\mathbf x^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta$ under the
linear model. For prediction, a natural estimand is the rule minimizing expected
loss in a specified target population. The ridge **estimator** is a random
function of the training sample; its fitted coefficients are the observed
**estimates**. They generally do not estimate the original coefficients without
bias.

Center $Y$ and every predictor so that the intercept can be omitted below. In
practice the intercept is estimated separately and is normally not penalized.
Predictors must also be put on meaningful, documented scales because the penalty
acts directly on coefficient magnitude.

# The Ridge Objective

For a tuning parameter $\lambda\geq0$, ridge solves

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}
=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\left\{\|\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2
+\lambda\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2\right\}.
}
$$

Some software divides the residual term by $n$, $2n$, or an estimate of
$\sigma^2$. Those conventions change the numerical value of $\lambda$, so tuning
parameters are not directly comparable across packages unless the objectives are
matched.

Differentiating the objective gives

$$
-2\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
+2\lambda\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf0,
$$

and therefore

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf I)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf y.
}
$$

When $\lambda>0$, adding $\lambda\mathbf I$ makes the matrix invertible even if
$p>n$ or $\mathbf X$ is rank deficient. At $\lambda=0$ the ordinary
least-squares solution is recovered when it is unique. As $\lambda$ increases,
slopes move continuously toward zero, but they are not normally set exactly to
zero.

An equivalent constrained form minimizes residual sum of squares subject to
$\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2\leq t$. Each nontrivial constraint corresponds to a
penalty value under suitable conditions. The spherical constraint explains why
ridge shares weight across correlated predictors rather than selecting a corner
of the parameter space.

# Singular-value Geometry

Let the centered design have singular-value decomposition

$$
\mathbf X=\mathbf U\mathbf D\mathbf V^\mathsf{T},
$$

with positive singular values $d_1,\ldots,d_r$. Then

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}
=\sum_{j=1}^{r}
\frac{d_j}{d_j^2+\lambda}
\mathbf v_j\mathbf u_j^\mathsf{T}\mathbf y.
$$

Ordinary least squares uses $1/d_j$ and can greatly amplify noise in directions
with small $d_j$. Ridge replaces that multiplier with
$d_j/(d_j^2+\lambda)$. Weakly supported directions are shrunk most strongly;
well-supported directions change less.

The fitted values are $\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf H_\lambda\mathbf y$, where

$$
\mathbf H_\lambda
=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf I)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}.
$$

A useful measure of model flexibility is

$$
\operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)
=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf H_\lambda)
=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\lambda}.
$$

It falls smoothly from the design rank toward zero as the penalty increases.
This is an effective degrees of freedom, not a count of nonzero coefficients.

# Bias, Variance, and Prediction Error

Conditioning on $\mathbf X$ under the linear model,

$$
E(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\mid\mathbf X)
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf I)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,
$$

so the estimator is biased toward zero when $\lambda>0$. Its covariance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\mid\mathbf X)
=\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf I)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X
(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf I)^{-1}.
$$

In the last display, the two inverse factors multiply the middle matrix; it is
not the inverse of their sum. Along singular direction $j$, the squared-bias and
variance contributions are controlled by $\lambda/(d_j^2+\lambda)$ and
$\sigma^2d_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda)^2$, respectively. A positive penalty can reduce
mean squared error when the variance reduction exceeds the added squared bias.

Prediction risk also depends on where future predictor vectors lie. Good
in-sample stabilization does not guarantee reliable extrapolation beyond the
training distribution.

# Bayesian Interpretation

With Gaussian errors and independent priors

$$
\beta_j\mid\sigma^2,\lambda
\sim N\!\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{\lambda}\right),
$$

the ridge solution is the posterior mode and, conditional on fixed
$\sigma^2$ and $\lambda$, also the posterior mean. This equivalence clarifies
that shrinkage encodes information: large coefficients are considered less
plausible a priori. It does not make a data-tuned penalty a fully specified
Bayesian analysis. A Bayesian workflow must account for uncertainty in prior
scales and examine posterior predictive adequacy.

# Choosing the Penalty

The penalty is part of the fitting algorithm and must be selected without using
the final test outcomes.

- **Cross-validation** estimates predictive loss for a stated resampling unit.
  Every preprocessing step, including normalization, imputation, feature
  filtering, and standardization, must be learned inside each training fold.
- **Generalized cross-validation** approximates leave-one-out error for linear
  smoothers using residual error and $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf H_\lambda)$.
- **Information criteria or empirical Bayes** can be useful when their likelihood
  and prior assumptions match the scientific problem.
- **Nested resampling** is required when an outer estimate of generalization
  error is wanted after tuning $\lambda$.

Choose folds at the independent-unit level. If several cells, aliquots, images,
or repeated measurements belong to one donor, they must remain together. For
site or time generalization, grouped or forward-chaining splits should mimic the
actual deployment task.

The minimum-error penalty and a more regularized penalty within one estimated
standard error of that minimum are common summaries. The latter is a heuristic,
not a universal inferential rule. Report the candidate grid, loss, fold
construction, and uncertainty across repeated splits.

# Scaling, Penalty Structure, and Coefficient Meaning

Standardizing each feature to unit sample standard deviation makes the default
penalty invariant to measurement units, but it changes the parameterization.
For skewed molecular features, robust or scientifically defined scales may be
more appropriate. Scales must be estimated from training data within resampling.

Not every coefficient should receive the same penalty. Intercepts, required
design variables, or prespecified confounders may be left unpenalized. Grouped
features, spline bases, and multi-level factors may need structured penalties to
avoid arbitrary treatment of their coding columns. Penalty factors should be
specified from the modeling goal, not adjusted until a favored result appears.

A ridge coefficient is conditional on all included variables, their scaling,
the penalty, and the training distribution. Its magnitude is not a direct rank
of biological importance. Correlated features can substitute for one another,
and shrinkage can distribute their shared signal across many coefficients.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity Analysis

| Question | Check | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Is the linear mean structure adequate? | residual-versus-fitted plots, nonlinear terms, held-out calibration | regularization does not repair misspecification |
| Is the penalty stable? | repeated grouped cross-validation and the full error curve | a flat curve implies that one selected $\lambda$ is not uniquely supported |
| Are predictions driven by a few units? | influence checks and leave-group-out refits | shrinkage reduces but does not eliminate leverage |
| Does preprocessing leak information? | audit every fold-specific transformation | leakage makes validation error optimistic |
| Are coefficients sensitive to scaling? | compare scientifically defensible scaling rules | the $L_2$ penalty is scale dependent |
| Is the target population represented? | compare predictor support across training and target units | ridge does not solve dataset shift or extrapolation |

Sensitivity analyses can compare penalty grids, scaling choices, inclusion of
required covariates, plausible feature filters, and grouped split definitions.
Assess predictions and scientifically relevant contrasts, not only the visual
smoothness of coefficient paths.

# Worked Bioinformatics Example

Suppose gene expression from $p=5{,}000$ prespecified genes is used to predict a
continuous drug-response phenotype in 120 patient-derived organoids. Multiple
organoids may come from the same donor, and each organoid may have technical
sequencing replicates.

The donor is the experimental unit for a new-donor prediction claim. Technical
libraries from the same organoid can improve measurement, but they do not create
independent donors. A defensible workflow groups all observations from one donor
within the same fold, learns normalization and gene scaling from each training
fold, tunes $\lambda$ internally, and evaluates the locked pipeline on held-out
donors or an external cohort.

Statistically, a reduction in held-out squared error supports the predictive
value of the complete regularized rule for the sampled target population.
Biologically, nonzero ridge coefficients do not establish that all represented
genes regulate drug response. Perturbation experiments, transportability across
laboratories, and pathway-level evidence are separate requirements.

  add a sparsity-inducing $L_1$ component.
- [Maximum a posteriori estimation](../statistical-inference/maximum-a-posteriori-estimation.qmd)
  provides the general prior-penalty connection.

1. Ridge adds a quadratic penalty that stabilizes weak design directions and
   remains computable when $p>n$.
2. The estimator is biased; improved prediction is possible when variance falls
   more than squared bias rises.
3. Scaling, penalty factors, preprocessing, and the choice of $\lambda$ are part
   of the model and must be reproduced inside validation.
4. Ridge usually retains every feature and cannot identify a unique mechanism
   among correlated predictors.
5. Biological replication at the target prediction unit determines effective
   sample size; technical replication does not replace it.
